<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

<span class="ltx_personname">Paul Debevec
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Netflix Eyeline Studios
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">A versatile video depth estimation model should (1) be accurate and consistent across frames, (2) produce high-resolution depth maps, and (3) support real-time streaming.
We propose FlashDepth, a method that satisfies all three requirements, performing depth estimation on a 2044<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>1148 streaming video at 24 FPS.
We show that, with careful modifications to pretrained single-image depth models, these capabilities are enabled with relatively little data and training.
We evaluate our approach across multiple unseen datasets against state-of-the-art depth models, and find that ours outperforms them in terms of boundary sharpness and speed by a significant margin, while maintaining competitive accuracy.
We hope our model will enable various applications that require high-resolution depth, such as video editing, and online decision-making, such as robotics.
We release all code and model weights at <a href="https://github.com/Eyeline-Research/FlashDepth" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">https://github.com/Eyeline-Research/FlashDepth</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<div id="id1" class="ltx_logical-block">
    
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para"><img src="2504.07093v2/teaser.png" id="g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:679/375;" width="679" height="375" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
    
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We present FlashDepth, a video depth estimation model that processes high-resolution streaming videos in real-time.
Given an in-the-wild video shown above (left column: original input and output; right column: zoomed-in), our method processes it in a streaming fashion at <span id="S0.F1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2044<math id="S0.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>1148</span> resolution at <span id="S0.F1.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">24 FPS</span>. In contrast, the state-of-the-art video depth model, DepthCrafter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, runs at 2.1 FPS at 1024<math id="S0.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>576 resolution and requires optimizing 110 images at once. Concurrent works like CUT3R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite> supports streaming inputs (512<math id="S0.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>288 at 14 FPS) but produces blurry depth; Video Depth Anything (VidDepthAny) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> runs at 24 FPS at 924<math id="S0.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>518 resolution but requires optimizing 32 images at once. Our predicted depth maps are noticeably sharper than all baselines, capturing thin structures such as tree leaves and fur. Zoom in for best viewing results.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
  
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>* This work was conducted during Gene’s internship at Netflix Eyeline Studios.</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Video depth estimation is a cornerstone for applications such as robotics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, augmented reality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>, and video editing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>.
Robots need real-time sensor data to make online decisions, augmented reality devices must provide streaming, consistent depth, and video editing such as object insertion requires high-resolution and precise depth maps.
As such, we identify three key characteristics
of a video depth estimation model that can support a wide range of applications: 1) consistency and accuracy across a video sequence, 2) the ability to preserve high-resolution and sharp features, and 3) real-time streaming.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Existing methods cannot satisfy all three requirements.
The most consistent and accurate video depth models rely on post-optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> or expensive video diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>. They are slow and can be computationally prohibitive to scale to higher resolutions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Methods that support real-time and streaming inputs are inaccurate because they rely on lightweight models that have limited network capacity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>, or are inconsistent because they cannot share contextual information between frames <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. These methods also become at least 3.5x slower <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> than real-time
at 2K resolution due to computational bottlenecks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we present FlashDepth, a model that
satisfies all three requirements.
Given a streaming video input at 2K resolution,<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          We refer to 2K resolution as the long side containing over 2000 pixels. For instance, Digital Cinema Initiatives defines a 2K format with a resolution of 2048<math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>1080. Our method runs at 24 FPS up to 2044<math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>1148 resolution (patch size 14, aspect ratio 1.78) on an A100 GPU.</span></span></span> it processes all pixels at 24 FPS on an A100 GPU.
It produces depth maps with high accuracy and sharp boundaries across multiple unseen datasets and in-the-wild videos, shown in <a href="#S0.F1" title="In FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#S2.F2" title="In Concurrent Work. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We achieve this by building on top of a state-of-the-art single-image depth model, Depth Anything v2 (DAv2) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>, rather than finetuning video diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>. While the latter approach achieves consistency for free, DAv2 is meticulously trained on large amounts of synthetic and real data and across multiple stages with multiple losses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>.
Its per-frame depth accuracy is significantly higher, while maintaining a lightweight architecture that is essential for real-time performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We enhance DAv2 with two key technical contributions. First, we add a recurrent neural network that aligns intermediate depth features of individual frames to the same scale, on-the-fly. An accurate relative depth map differs from the ground truth only by a scale and shift factor, so determining the correct scaling factors for each individual depth map aligns them to the same scale. We hypothesize that a lightweight recurrent network is sufficient for this task, but we align the intermediate features, which are computationally cheaper to handle, rather than the final depth maps. We empirically find that this simple approach generalizes to long sequences, moving objects, and large camera pose changes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Second, we design a hybrid model that balances quality and efficiency. The runtime of DAv2 scales with resolution;
it processes 2K frames at a slow 6 FPS. Our hybrid model features a lightweight component that processes the full 2K resolution to preserve sharp boundaries, but fuses more accurate features from a computationally intensive component that runs at lower resolution.
This approach is motivated by the observation that the raw accuracy of depth maps (i.e., estimating the correct depth relationships between pixels) is less dependent on resolution because boundaries that separate foreground and background account for less than 1% of pixels, on average, but getting sharp boundaries requires high-resolution processing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We validate our method and design choices through extensive experiments. We will release all code and model weights.
In short, we make the following findings and contributions:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a real-time method to estimate depth for streaming videos at 2K resolution, supporting applications that require high-resolution and realism.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our method to the state-of-the-art and find that it achieves competitive accuracy across multiple datasets, even compared to methods that process large batches of images at once (as opposed to streaming).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We build on open-source pretrained models and require relatively little additional data, making our method easy to train and circumventing the shortage of high-quality video depth data.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Depth Estimation from a Single Image.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advances in single-image depth models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> have been enabled by large amounts of data, both real <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite> and synthetic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, and by scalable pretrained architectures, such as vision transformers (ViTs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> and diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>.
However, single-image models produce flickering, inconsistent depth when applied per-frame to a video sequence. This is true even for metric depth prediction models because of the inherent ambiguity given only a single image.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Optimization-based Video Depth Estimation.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Another common approach is to optimize depth for multiple images jointly. Such methods include classic and learnable dense visual SLAM
methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite>, as well as methods that optimize the outputs of single-image models to a global scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>.
BTimer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> produces a reconstruction in a single forward pass, but requires the entire video as input.
Prompt Depth Anything <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>
aligns relative depth to sparse, low-resolution LiDAR to produce 4K depth maps but relies on external sensors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Another line of recent work estimates pointmaps (e.g., DUSt3R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>), from which depth maps and camera parameters can be computed.
Follow-up work shows that these methods can generalize to videos and dynamic scenes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>, but they still require a global bundle adjustment optimization.
We compare to state-of-the-art pointmap estimation method, and find that they achieve lower depth accuracy and sharpness compared to dedicated depth prediction models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Optimization-based methods can produce consistent and accurate depths across a sequence, but are either slow or can only approach real-time speeds at low-resolution (e.g., DROID-SLAM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite> averages 15 FPS at 240<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>320).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Online Video Depth Estimation.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To the best of our knowledge, there are relatively few methods that perform real-time online depth estimation (i.e., operate when only one frame is given at a time). <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> attempt this setting with LSTMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> stores a global point cloud to maintain consistency.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite> predicts stereo and motion cues. However, these methods cannot scale to high-resolution frames without substantial changes to their architecture.
In addition, these methods have only been trained and tested on small datasets and produce depth maps with low accuracy and high flicker <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Aside from the architectural limitations, a likely reason for the poor performance of prior methods is a shortage of video data with moving objects, diverse camera poses, and ground truth depth.
Among the limited options, self-driving datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> contain sparse depth with small changes in camera motion, while synthetic scenes with moving objects have limited scene diversity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Although our approach to enforcing consistency is similar to this class of methods (i.e., we also use a recurrent network to perform online alignment), we revisit this problem setting with modern architectures and training approaches. Our design circumvents the shortage of data and outperforms many state-of-the-art baselines.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Video Depth Estimation using Diffusion Models.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At the time of writing, most state-of-the-art video depth models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite> finetune video diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> due to their strong consistency and motion priors, compensating for the lack of abundant, high-quality data.
These methods strike a balance between optimization-based and online approaches because they generally do not take the full video as input but still must process batches of frames, followed by stitching or optimization to align each batch.
While these methods demonstrate impressive generalization and accuracy, it is non-trivial to scale them to real-time, high-resolution depth due to the compute demands of diffusion models at inference-time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Concurrent Work.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Video Depth Anything <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> and CUT3R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite> are two relevant concurrent works.
Like our method, Video Depth Anything finetunes Depth Anything v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> on video data with a temporal module. However, their method requires processing batches of 32 images at once, so it does not support streaming and becomes computationally prohibitive to scale in resolution.
CUT3R can handle streaming inputs, but depth maps produced from their pointmaps are of lower quality than those of a dedicated depth estimation model.
We compare our method to both of these works in <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2504.07093v2/wild_visualizations.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/487;" width="685" height="487" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We visualize predicted depth maps (top row) of each method on in-the-wild videos. We also zoom-in (green bounding boxes) to emphasize the boundaries (bottom row). Our method processes high-resolution frames natively and produces sharper boundaries, especially for thin structures and small or far objects.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2504.07093v2/archv2.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:316/279;" width="316" height="279" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Our architecture builds on DPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> and Depth Anything v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>, but is designed for
streaming videos.
A recurrent network (Mamba <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>) aligns frames to a consistent scale on-the-fly, and our hybrid model scales to 2K resolution while maintaining accuracy and throughput of 24 FPS.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FlashDepth builds on a pretrained single-image depth model to estimate accurate depth for each individual frame, and enforces consistency for a streaming video in an autoregressive manner.
In <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Single-Image Depth Base Model ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we
describe Depth Anything v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>, our base model. In <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Enforcing Temporal Consistency ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> we explain our approach to enforcing temporal consistency.
In <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Hybrid Model for Efficiency at High-Resolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, we explain our strategy for training a hybrid model to handle 2K resolution videos while maintaining throughput and accuracy.
We provide a diagram of our architecture in <a href="#S2.F3" title="In Concurrent Work. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Single-Image Depth Base Model</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use
Depth Anything v2 (DAv2) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> as our single-image base model, which consists of a pretrained DINOv2 ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> encoder and a DPT decoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>.
An image is tokenized and passed through the ViT for feature extraction.
Four intermediate features layers from the ViT, specifically the outputs of layers 5, 12, 18, and 24 from a 24-layer model, are collected and passed to the DPT decoder.
The motivation is that shallow layers contain more spatial details, while deep layers contain more semantic information.
The DPT decoder fuses these features using residual convolutional units <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> to produce a depth map.
DAv2 can produce highly detailed and accurate depth maps, but running it on a sequence of frames leads to flickering because there is no common scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Enforcing Temporal Consistency</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To maintain consistent depths across frames, our approach is driven by three considerations.
First, the model should handle streaming inputs, which means it only has access to the current frame and past information.
One way to achieve this is using a recurrent network (e.g., an RNN).
The recurrent network maintains a hidden state that encodes information from past frames and updates this hidden state when a new frame arrives.
Specifically, we use Mamba <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> because it has been shown to
selectively retain relevant information over long sequences.
Our Mamba module processes features from the DPT decoder, and aligns the features while storing context.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Second, we want the scale alignment to incur negligible overhead.
We assume dense pixel-level features are unnecessary for aligning depths across frames, so we downsample the DPT decoder’s feature output before processing it with Mamba, reducing computational load.
The alignment operation can be written as</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_gather ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle f,H_{t}=\text{Mamba}(\text{Flatten}(\operatorname{Down}(F)),H_{t-1})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Mamba</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>Flatten</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Down</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle f,H_{t}=\text{Mamba}(\text{Flatten}(\operatorname{Down}(F)),H_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle F_{\text{align}}=F+\operatorname{Up}(\text{UnFlatten}(f))," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mtext>align</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>Up</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>UnFlatten</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle F_{\text{align}}=F+\operatorname{Up}(\text{UnFlatten}(f)),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> is the feature output from the DPT decoder with shape <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B,C,H,W)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B,C,H,W)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is Mamba’s hidden state at time <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, Flatten reshapes a 4D tensor from <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B,C,H,W)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B,C,H,W)</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B,H\times W,C)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B,H\times W,C)</annotation></semantics></math>, UnFlatten reverses Flatten, and Down and Up indicate bilinear downsampling and upsampling operations, respectively.
<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\text{align}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mtext>align</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\text{align}}</annotation></semantics></math> is then passed through the final convolution head to produce a depth map.
Our temporal module consists of roughly 1% of the total parameters of our model.
It adds negligible overhead in practice due to its small size and the input’s reduced context length after downsampling.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Third, we want to initialize our temporal module such that it maintains the performance of the base single-image depth model.
To achieve this, we place the Mamba model after the DPT decoder, only before the final convolution head, to preserve the integrity of the pretrained features.
We zero-initialize the output layer of the Mamba model so that the first iteration of FlashDepth remains a valid depth map.
This preserves the original capabilities of the model at initialization while allowing the training procedure to gradually nudge it toward our consistency objective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, our pipeline processes each input image individually through the ViT encoder and DPT decoder to produce a feature map.
Subsequently, the Mamba module adjusts each feature map and updates its hidden state, given the features of the current frame.
Finally, the adjusted features pass through the convolution head to generate consistent depth predictions.
This pipeline is illustrated in <a href="#S2.F3" title="In Concurrent Work. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (so far, we have described only the high-resolution path through ViT-S).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Hybrid Model for Efficiency at High-Resolution</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While our temporal module adds negligible latency, the original model (DAv2-Large) achieves only 6 FPS at 2K resolution.
It is difficult to simultaneously scale up both model size and resolution while achieving real-time performance.
To address this, we examine the runtime and accuracy trade-off across the existing DAv2 family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>, which includes three checkpoints—DAv2-Small (S), DAv2-Base (B), and DAv2-Large (L)—finetuned from DINOv2’s ViT-Small, ViT-Base, and ViT-Large backbones, respectively.
DAv2-L achieves the highest accuracy across all benchmarks but is slow at high resolution.
Conversely, DAv2-S achieves real-time throughput at 2K resolution but yields a substantial accuracy drop, so directly reducing the model size is an inadequate solution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To achieve real-time depth estimation at 2K resolution without compromising accuracy, we propose a hybrid model that processes frames in two streams, based on the following considerations.
First, for real-time throughput, the main stream that processes 2K frames must be lightweight. We denote this stream FlashDepth-S, finetuned from DAv2-S and adding our temporal module.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Second, to maintain accuracy, we incorporate the features from a more powerful model, namely DAv2-L. We train a second stream FlashDepth-L that finetunes DAv2-L and processes frames at a lower resolution (518px) to produce accurate features that can be used to supervise the intermediate features of FlashDepth-S.
We use cross-attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite> to fuse the intermediate features without modifying the original architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We observe that while resolution is crucial for preserving sharp boundaries, it has minimal impact on numerical accuracy, since boundaries account for less than 1% of pixels, on average. For instance, we test the per-frame accuracy of DAv2 on multiple datasets at 2K vs 518px (resizing short side to 518 while maintaining aspect ratio) resolution, and find that the difference in accuracy between the two is negligible. However, we start seeing degradation in accuracy at even lower resolutions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We show this pipeline in <a href="#S2.F3" title="In Concurrent Work. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. A high-resolution image (2044<math id="S3.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>1148) is passed through FlashDepth-S.
Concurrently, a downsampled image (924<math id="S3.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>518) is passed through FlashDepth-L.
The intermediate features from the larger model are fused with those of the smaller model:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\text{fused}_{i}}=\text{CrossAttn}(Q=F_{\text{S}_{i}},KV=F_{\text{L}_{i}})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><msub><mtext>fused</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>CrossAttn</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><msub><mtext>S</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><msub><mtext>L</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\text{fused}_{i}}=\text{CrossAttn}(Q=F_{\text{S}_{i}},KV=F_{\text{L}_{i}}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\text{S}_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><msub><mtext>S</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\text{S}_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\text{L}_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><msub><mtext>L</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\text{L}_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote intermediate feature representations at the <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th layer of the DPT decoders from the small and large models, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We zero-initialize the module such that at the first training iteration, <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\text{fused}_{i}}=F_{\text{S}_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><msub><mtext>fused</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><msub><mtext>S</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\text{fused}_{i}}=F_{\text{S}_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This encourages FlashDepth-S to gradually learn to use <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\text{L}_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><msub><mtext>L</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\text{L}_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> without abrupt changes to its learned weights.
The cross-attention module is lightweight and processes a sequence length of <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times N</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is the sequence length of the high-resolution image features, and <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the sequence length of the base-resolution image features (the output of the first DPT layer maintains the same sequence length as the input to the transformer).
By training this hybrid model on small amounts of video depth data, it learns to use the cross-attention module to extract the more accurate features, while preserving sharpness and speed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">By running both models concurrently, even with communication between the two, we can process 2K images at 24 FPS (wall time) on an A100 GPU.
Empirically, we show that our hybrid model’s accuracy is comparable to that of FlashDepth-L (<a href="#S4.T2" title="In Datasets. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), and is noticeably higher than that of FlashDepth-S (<a href="#S4.T4" title="In 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Two Stage Training</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training our model end-to-end requires a large number of videos with high-resolution dense depth maps, but most existing datasets are sub-720p.
Instead, we train our model in two stages.
First, we use low-resolution depth data to train FlashDepth-L and FlashDepth-S (<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Enforcing Temporal Consistency ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>) to be consistent across video sequences.
Then, we use a small amount of high-resolution data to supervise a hybrid model (<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Hybrid Model for Efficiency at High-Resolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) initialized from FlashDepth-L and FlashDepth-S.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the first stage, we initialize the ViT encoders and DPT decoders of FlashDepth-L and FlashDepth-S from DAv2-L and DAv2-S, respectively, and train the temporal modules from scratch.
We use the following datasets: MVS-Synth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, Spring <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, TartanAir <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite>, PointOdyssey <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite>, and Dynamic Replica <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>. After filtering out invalid scenes, we obtain roughly half a million image-depth pairs. We process all frames to a fixed resolution of <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="518\times 518" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>518</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>518</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">518\times 518</annotation></semantics></math> via random cropping.
Since these datasets are synthetic and metric, we supervise our model using a simple L1 loss, instead of the scale-shift-invariant loss used by many prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>.
We do not use any additional supervision, such as optical flow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> or temporal losses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Due to memory constraints, we perform backpropagation with input sequences containing a small number of frames, but augment the dataset by setting longer strides between frames.
This allows our model to maintain consistency when tested on videos containing up to 1000 frames, and even outperform state-of-the-art video depth models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> that perform an explicit optimization designed to stitch shorter sequences into longer ones.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In the second stage,
we train our hybrid model using two high-resolution depth datasets with 2K depth annotations: MVS-Synth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> and Spring <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, which contains a total of roughly 16,000 image-depth pairs.
We freeze the weights in FlashDepth-L and only finetune FlashDepth-S.
FlashDepth-S processes images at their original 2K resolution, and FlashDepth-L processes the downsampled version (short side 518) of the input images.
We initialize the cross-attention blocks that transfer features between the DPT decoders from scratch.
Again, we supervise this model using an L1 loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S2.F3" title="In Concurrent Work. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, only the intermediate features from DPT, rather than from Mamba, are taken from FlashDepth-L, but training FlashDepth-L in the first stage is crucial for aligning the features of FlashDepth-L and FlashDepth-S to roughly the same scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each of our Mamba modules <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.2 Enforcing Temporal Consistency ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> consists of four blocks.
Each block contains layer normalization, a Mamba layer, and an MLP.
Empirically, we found that a vanilla Mamba implementation, rather than a bidirectional scan <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>]</cite>, is sufficient for our task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The CrossAttn module in <a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3.3 Hybrid Model for Efficiency at High-Resolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> consists of two transformer blocks with cross-attention. It takes queries (Q) from the high-resolution features (<math id="S3.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\text{S}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mtext>S</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\text{S}}</annotation></semantics></math>), and keys and values (KV) from the low-resolution, but more accurate features (<math id="S3.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\text{L}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mtext>L</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\text{L}}</annotation></semantics></math>). We only fuse the output features of the first DPT layers to avoid low resolution artifacts seeping into the high-resolution stream.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">During first-stage training, we set the Mamba learning rates to 1e-4, and the rest of the model to 1e-6.
Each takes half a day on 8 A100 GPUs. During the second stage, we freeze FlashDepth-L, set the cross-attention module’s learning rate to 1e-4, and finetune the FlashDepth-S model with learning rate 1e-6. This also takes half a day on 8 A100 GPUs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">During inference, we load one image at a time. Since this does not fully utilize the GPU, we can create CUDA graphs to run the two streams (up to the cross-attention module) in parallel. Additionally, our method defaults to running FlashDepth-L directly when the short side of the image has fewer than 518 pixels, since it is capable of running in real-time at that resolution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To facilitate reproduction, we will release all code and model weights.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2504.07093v2/results-compressed.png" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:679/636;" width="679" height="636" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We provide more results of predicted depth maps (top row) on high-quality synthetic datasets (UnrealStereo4K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite> and UrbanSyn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>) and zoom-in (green bounding boxes) to show the edge maps (bottom row), which are defined by a depth value change between neighboring pixels, above a threshold. This allows us to quantitatively evaluate the predicted boundaries with ground truth depth (<a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Depth Sharpness, Resolution, and Runtime ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>). Compared to baselines, our method captures thin structures and small or far objects.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our method to DepthCrafter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, Video Depth Anything <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, CUT3R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>, and Depth Anything v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>.
DepthCrafter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> is finetuned from a video diffusion model and demonstrates strong generalization
and higher accuracy compared to previous video depth models, such as ChronoDepth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> and NVDS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>.
Video Depth Anything (VidDepthAny) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> is concurrent work that finetunes Depth Anything v2 (DAv2) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> with a temporal module. For all experiments, we use their largest model.
CUT3R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite> is also concurrent work that estimates pointmaps from streaming videos by designing a transformer-based recurrent model.
We include DAv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> because it is the base model of VidDepthAny and our method, and serves as a reference point for understanding the effects of our approaches. For all experiments, we use their DAv2-Large model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each scene, we denote with <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{d}</annotation></semantics></math> the predicted depths across the sequence with shape <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B,h,w)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B,h,w)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of frames in the scene, and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> the ground truth depth, with shape <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B,H,W)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B,H,W)</annotation></semantics></math>. Following standard practice, we run each method on its default resolution (<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h,w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h,w</annotation></semantics></math>), which is either the default resolution provided in their code, or the resolution it was trained on, while maintaining aspect ratio.
Then we bilinear interpolate the outputs to <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H,W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H,W</annotation></semantics></math> and use least squares to find a scale and shift factor to align the entire predicted sequence with ground truth (as opposed to finding a per-frame scale and shift).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use three metrics. The first two measure accuracy (<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{1}\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{1}\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>) and relative error (AbsRel <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>), defined as
<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{1}=\text{percentage of pixels where}\max(d/\hat{d},\hat{d}/d)&lt;1.25)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>percentage of pixels where</mtext><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>/</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1.25</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{1}=\text{percentage of pixels where}\max(d/\hat{d},\hat{d}/d)&lt;1.25)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AbsRel}=|\hat{d}-d|/d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>AbsRel</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AbsRel}=|\hat{d}-d|/d</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.
The third is the boundary metric proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>: if the ground truth neighboring pixels differ by a threshold, we classify it as an boundary, and we calculate the F1 score to determine whether the predicted depths have the same classification. We provide more details in the supplement. This metric focuses on fine details and sharp boundaries, which tend not to be measured in error and accuracy metrics because the boundaries represent just 1% of pixels, on average. We show depth maps and their corresponding boundary maps in <a href="#S2.F2" title="In Concurrent Work. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S3.F4" title="In 3.5 Implementation Details ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We test on five diverse datasets. ETH3D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite> contains 13 real scenes, both outdoor and indoor. Sintel <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> is a 3D animated film with many moving objects. Waymo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> is a self-driving dataset with continuous camera motion. We randomly sampled 30 scenes from its validation set. Unreal4K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite> and UrbanSyn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> are both synthetic but photorealistic datasets with diverse camera viewpoints and scenes.
Unreal4k has nine scenes in total, whereas UrbanSyn contains a total of more than 7,000 frames.
We take the first 1,000 frames of UrbanSyn as our testing data.
Even though the images in ETH3D, Unreal4k, and UrbanSyn are not organized as continuous video sequences, we stitch these images into a video to mimic video frames with significant camera motion.
We compute both relative error and absolute accuracy metrics in all five datasets.
We report boundary sharpness using only Unreal4k and UrbanSyn, since only these two contain dense and high-resolution ground truth depth maps.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T1.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">We report the F1 score of predicted vs ground truth boundaries, defined by a value change between neighboring pixels, across multiple thresholds.
For all methods, we use their default resolution (i.e., the resolution provided in their demo or used during training) while preserving aspect ratio. We also report the corresponding FPS when run at the denoted resolution, over 1000 frames. Results validate that processing frames natively at high-resolution is crucial for preserving fine details (FlashDepth-L vs FlashDepth-L (high)). <sup id="S4.T1.9.1" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup> means the method does not support streaming, but process batches of images instead.
</span></figcaption>

<td id="S4.T2.3.8.12" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T2.3.8.12.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">3.4</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>We compare error and accuracy metrics across five diverse datasets. The number next to the dataset name is the number of frames in each scene. The predicted depth is aligned with ground truth using a global scale and shift along the sequence to calculate metrics. <sup id="S4.T2.14" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup> means the method does not support streaming, but process batches of images instead. <span id="S4.T2.15" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">Gray</span> means the method was trained on the test data. Based on the average <math id="S4.T2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> rank, our method’s accuracy only trails behind that of Video Depth Anything <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> (concurrent work), which optimizes batches of 32 images, while ours handles streaming inputs (i.e., one frame at a time).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Depth Sharpness, Resolution, and Runtime</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first evaluate the boundary sharpness and runtime of each method, which is the focus of ours, and crucial for online tasks and applications that require high-resolution.
We use the F1 score proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. The boundaries are defined by a value difference between neighboring pixels, and we calculate these boundaries across multiple thresholds.
We visualize the boundaries of a fixed threshold as an example in <a href="#S2.F3" title="In Concurrent Work. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Our method captures thin structures like poles and leaves and overall produces sharper boundaries compared to existing methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the four baselines, we include results for our full hybrid model (FlashDepth (Full)), large model (FlashDepth-L), and the large model run at higher resolution large model (FlashDepth-L (high)).
We report quantitative results in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In Datasets. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Boundary sharpness is correlated to resolution, as a low-resolution image blurs or averages out boundaries. Thus, it is not surprising that FlashDepth (Full) significantly outperforms baselines as it operates at a higher resolution. However, FlashDepth-L (high) also produces sharper boundaries than FlashDepth (Full), showing that there also exists a tradeoff between model capacity and boundary sharpness, even if resolution seems to be the most important factor.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing video depth models cannot be easily extended to higher resolutions. DepthCrafter and VidDepthAny process 110 and 32 frames, respectively, and run out of memory at higher resolutions. For instance, running VidDepthAny at 924<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>518 resolution takes up 40gb of vram. CUT3R is only trained on resolutions under 518px (long side 518), and performance degrades at higher resolutions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We also report the FPS in wall time at the denoted resolutions. For a scene in Unreal4k with 1000 images, we start the timer after a single warmup iteration, and record the time after all frames are processed.
From our experiments, only our hybrid approach is capable of operating at high-resolution while maintaining real-time performance of 24 FPS.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Depth Error and Accuracy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report all error and accuracy metrics in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In Datasets. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
All methods are run at the resolution reported in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In Datasets. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
While we visualize per-frame depth maps in <a href="#S2.F3" title="In Concurrent Work. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we encourage readers to view our supplemental videos to visualize each method’s consistency over video sequences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">VidDepthAny achieves the overall highest accuracy across the five datasets, with our base model coming in second. VidDepthAnything processes 32 images at once while ours only sees one frame at a time, but still demonstrates competitive performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">DepthCrafter is finetuned from a video diffusion model and processes 110 images at once, but our method produces higher accuracy across all but one datasets. Since we align the entire sequence to ground truth using only a global scale and shift for comparison, this shows that our temporal module can align streaming frames to the same scale without an expensive model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our method also performs better than CUT3R, even though CUT3R was trained on 33 datasets.
This indicates that building on top of a dedicated, pretrained depth estimation model with small amounts of data can significantly simplify training while achieving high performance, compared to training from scratch.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Both VidDepthAny and our method perform better than DAv2 on all datasets, up to a 20% increase in accuracy in many cases, showing that a temporal alignment (regardless of the implementation) is a promising direction for generalizing single-image models to the video domain, rather than relying on expensive video diffusion models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">By comparing the two variations of FlashDepth, we verify that our cross-attention module successfully transfers the robust features predicted by the base model. FlashDepth (Full) is ranked third among the methods, and generally trails behind its counterpart FlashDepth-L by only 1-2%. Note that, as mentioned in <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5 Implementation Details ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>, FlashDepth (Full) defaults to running FlashDepth-L when the short side of the image has less than 518 pixels, so the metrics for Sintel are the same for both methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, we show in <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a> that across all datasets, FlashDepth-S performs noticeably worse, validating that directly decreasing model capacity is not a desirable tradeoff.</p>
</div>
