<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T3.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.T3.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Ablation study of super-resolution methods. We report the accuracy (<math id="S4.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the F1 score of predicted vs. ground truth boundaries. Using the same base model (FlashDepth-L), we compare three ways to preserve boundary sharpness: a UNet, a guided-filter super-resolution network (DAGF), and ours. The outputs of all three methods have the same 2K resolution. Our hybrid model (FlashDepth (Full)) produces depth maps that are much sharper than other methods while preserving accuracy on test sets.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Ablation Study</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Super-Resolution vs Hybrid Model</span>.
Our hybrid model preserves accuracy and boundary sharpness while maintaining real-time performance.
But
can we simply use a dedicated depth super-resolution network?</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We examine a recent survey <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite> on depth super-resolution and find that even the most recent methods, whether they use diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> or learnable filters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>, overfit their models to single datasets and their reported numbers show unsatisfactory generalization. Although we did not find ablation studies that trained on multiple datasets, we hypothesize these models are unable to generalize because this requires training with diverse, high-quality data and sometimes multiple stages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We report quantitative results in <a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.2 Depth Error and Accuracy ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. FlashDepth-L is our baseline, where we bilinear upsample the 518px outputs to the ground truth resolution. “+ UNet” is one of our earlier experiments, where we pretrain FlashDepth-L on our five training datasets at 518px resolution, then freeze it and add a UNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> trained from scratch. The UNet encodes the high-resolution image, then uses skip connections to upsample the low-resolution depth map features (after our Mamba module and before the final convolution head, so the head is re-trained). We find that this approach hurts both accuracy and boundary sharpness, likely because there is insufficient data to re-train the head to match the performance of the pretrained one. In contrast, our hybrid approach ensures no modifications to the original capabilities of the model during the first training iteration, so it can be finetuned without a lot of data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We also compare to an off-the-shelf super-resolution network. We apply DAGF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>, which is a relatively fast method (10 FPS) that uses an attention-guided image filtering technique, to the output depth of FlashDepth-L (denoted “+ DAGF”). This led to substantially worse accuracy, dropping by roughly 20%. In line with the paper’s findings, the network cannot generalize to out-of-distribution data. It can only be run after FlashDepth-L, resulting in an 7.7 FPS.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">From <a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.2 Depth Error and Accuracy ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, FlashDepth (Full) not only preserves boundary sharpness from high-resolution images, but it also maintains accuracy and strong generalization due to the transfer of features from the more powerful FlashDepth-L. In contrast, neither learning-based nor filtering-based methods match our performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">From our observations, super-resolution methods show poor generalization performance, and may require substantial amounts of high-resolution training data to improve results, which are not easily obtainable. Our approach directly leverages pretrained single-image models to avoid this issue.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Ablation study of our hybrid model FlashDepth (Full) vs a smaller model FlashDepth-S. A smaller model is faster but at the cost of substantially decreased accuracy, as shown in this table: reducing the model size from FlashDepth-L to FlashDepth-S leads to a 3-10% drop. On the other hand, our hybrid model runs at the same speed as FlashDepth-S, at the cost of a noticeably smaller decrease in accuracy across all datasets.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FlashDepth (Full) vs FlashDepth-S</span>. In <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Hybrid Model for Efficiency at High-Resolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> we discuss the motivation for our hybrid model is that decreasing model size directly leads to a substantial accuracy drop, as shown in the original DAv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> paper. Here, we run an ablation to verify this observation. In <a href="#S4.T4" title="In 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we compare three variations of FlashDepth. We find that reducing the model size from FlashDepth-L (<math id="S4.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>300M parameters) to FlashDepth-S (<math id="S4.SS3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>21M parameters) leads to a 3-10% accuracy drop across all datasets. On the other hand, our hybrid model runs at the same speed as FlashDepth-S, at the cost of a noticeably smaller decrease (1-3%). This validates our design and confirms that our cross-attention module transfer more robust features from FlashDepth-L.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we develop a method that performs depth estimation of a 2048<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>1152 streaming video at 24 FPS. Compared to the state-of-the-art, our method delivers better boundary sharpness while being very competitive in terms of accuracy when processes streaming inputs in real time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The main limitation of our method is
residual flickering.
While it may be difficult to match the performance of online methods to that of optimization, it would be possible to concurrently optimize processed frames while streaming new ones for certain applications, similar to SLAM. We leave this for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>

<li id="bib.bib74" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem"><span id="bib.bib74.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[74]</span></span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span id="bib.bib74.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Lianghui Zhu, Bencheng Liao, Qian Zhang, Xinlong Wang, Wenyu Liu, and Xinggang Wang.
</span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span id="bib.bib74.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Vision mamba: Efficient visual representation learning with bidirectional state space model.
</span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span id="bib.bib74.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">In </span><em id="bib.bib74.10" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">ICML</em><span id="bib.bib74.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, 2024.
</span>
</span></li>
    
</ul>
</section>

<div id="p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:144%;">Supplementary Material 
<br class="ltx_break"></span></p>

<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Evaluating Temporal Consistency</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate temporal consistency, we record the optimal scale factor between each individual predicted depth map and its corresponding ground truth frame to measure the drift in scale.
Specifically, we use the Waymo test set, which consists of 200 frames per scene.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We provide a plot in <a href="#S6.F5" title="In 6 Evaluating Temporal Consistency ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, which shows the average standard deviation of scale factors across all test sequences from Waymo, where the frame index on the <math id="S6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-axis indicates the standard deviation of scale factors for the first <math id="S6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> video frames.
DepthCrafter yields the lowest numbers and is the most temporally consistent, though it is slow and cannot output high-resolution frames.
FlashDepth and CUT3R are comparable, likely because the mechanisms for handling new input frames both involve recurrent networks with a hidden state, though FlashDepth is more accurate.
On the other hand, VidDepthAny aligns every 32 frames without knowledge of previous frames. The standard deviation rapidly increases with the number of frames, showing it is unable to maintain long-range temporal consistency.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2504.07093v2/figures/temporal_std.png" id="S6.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:274/274;" width="274" height="274" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S6.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Standard deviations of scale averaged over all Waymo test sequences.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Ablation Study on Temporal Modules</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform an ablation study of the recurrent module in FlashDepth. Specifically, in addition to our original Mamba design, we evaluate xLSTM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> and a transformer-based recurrent network, following CUT3R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>. We show results in <a href="#S7.T5" title="In 7 Ablation Study on Temporal Modules ‣ FlashDepth: Real-time Streaming Video Depth Estimation at 2K Resolution" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across datasets, the accuracies are close, with Mamba achieving the highest scores the most times. Mamba is also slightly faster. This shows that the specific choice of recurrent network is not crucial to our method; one could swap out Mamba for future faster or more task-specific options.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While FlashDepth builds on existing components like Mamba and pretrained depth models, its technical novelty lies in the carefully designed integration of these modules to tackle the challenging setting of online, real-time, high-resolution depth estimation.</p>
</div>

<table id="S7.T5.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Evaluation Details</h2>

<section id="S8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">8.1 </span>F1 Score for Boundary Sharpness</h3>

<div id="S8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow the F1 metric proposed in Depth Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.
Here, we provide the definition taken from the paper:</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use the pairwise depth ratio of neighboring pixels to define a foreground/background relationship.
Let <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i,j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i,j</annotation></semantics></math> be the locations of two neighboring pixels. We then define an occluding contour <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> derived from a depth map <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="c_{d}(i,j)=\left[\tfrac{d(j)}{d(i)}&gt;(1+\tfrac{t}{100})\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mn>100</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{d}(i,j)=\left[\tfrac{d(j)}{d(i)}&gt;(1+\tfrac{t}{100})\right]</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\cdot]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\cdot]</annotation></semantics></math> is the Iverson bracket. Intuitively, this indicates the presence of an occluding contour between pixels <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> if their corresponding depth differs by more than <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
For all pairs of neighboring pixels, we can then compute the precision (<math id="S8.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>) and recall (<math id="S8.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>) as</p>
<table id="S8.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_gather ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S8.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S8.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{P}(t)=\frac{\sum_{i,j\in N(i)}c_{d}(i,j)\wedge c_{\hat{d}}(i,j)}{\sum_{i,j\in N(i)}c_{d}(i,j)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>P</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>∧</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{P}(t)=\frac{\sum_{i,j\in N(i)}c_{d}(i,j)\wedge c_{\hat{d}}(i,j)}{\sum_{i,j\in N(i)}c_{d}(i,j)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S8.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S8.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{R}(t)=\frac{\sum_{i,j\in N(i)}c_{d}(i,j)\wedge c_{\hat{d}}(i,j)}{\sum_{i,j\in N(i)}c_{\hat{d}}(i,j)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>R</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>∧</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{R}(t)=\frac{\sum_{i,j\in N(i)}c_{d}(i,j)\wedge c_{\hat{d}}(i,j)}{\sum_{i,j\in N(i)}c_{\hat{d}}(i,j)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S8.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Note that both <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> are scale-invariant. In our experiments, we report the F1 score.
To account for multiple relative depth ratios,
we further perform a weighted averaging of the F1 values with 10 thresholds that range linearly from <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{min}=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{min}=5</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S8.SS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{max}=25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{max}=25</annotation></semantics></math>,
with stronger weights towards high threshold values.
This metric does not require any manual edge annotation,
but simply pixelwise ground truth, which is easily obtained for synthetic datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">8.2 </span>Measuring FPS in Wall Time</h3>

<div id="S8.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All FPS numbers were reported using the same machine on a single A100 GPU, with float16 precision. We preprocess all 1000 images to the appropriate resolutions and load them onto GPU memory before starting inference. We start the timer after a single warmup iteration: <math id="S8.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\verb|torch.cuda.synchronize;start=time.time()|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace" mathvariant="monospace">torch.cuda.synchronize;start=time.time()</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\verb|torch.cuda.synchronize;start=time.time()|</annotation></semantics></math> and we stop the timer only after all frames have been processed and aligned as needed: <math id="S8.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\verb|torch.cuda.synchronize;end=time.time()|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace" mathvariant="monospace">torch.cuda.synchronize;end=time.time()</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\verb|torch.cuda.synchronize;end=time.time()|</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We note that our FPS for VidDepthAny is different from that reported on its official repo.
We were able to match their FPS of 71 on a tensor of shape 1 <math id="S8.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 32 <math id="S8.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 518 <math id="S8.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 518, but we recorded 24 FPS across the entire sequence of shape 1 <math id="S8.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 1000 <math id="S8.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 924 <math id="S8.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 518. Reasons for the discrepancy include the increase in resolution and that that VidDepthAny sets an overlap of 10 images between batches to perform alignment, so the model actually has to process 1504 frames through a sliding window, despite a fixed video length of 1000.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>
</div>
